sec.title: Objective
sec.p: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is often associated with neuropsychiatric symptoms, including agitation and aggressive behavior. These symptoms increase with disease severity, ranging from 10% in mild cognitive impairment to 50% in patients with moderate‐to‐severe AD, pose a great risk for self‐injury and injury to caregivers, result in high rates of institutionalization and great suffering for patients and families. Current pharmacological therapies have limited efficacy and a high potential for severe side effects. Thus, there is a growing need to develop novel therapeutics tailored to safely and effectively reduce agitation and aggressive behavior in AD. Here, we investigate for the first time the use of focused ultrasound combined with anesthetic‐loaded nanodroplets (nanoFUS) targeting the amygdala (key structure in the neurocircuitry of agitation) as a novel minimally invasive tool to modulate local neural activity and reduce agitation and aggressive behavior in the TgCRND8 AD transgenic mice.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Male and female animals were tested in the resident‐intruder (i.e., aggressive behavior) and open‐field tests (i.e., motor agitation) for baseline measures, followed by treatment with active‐ or sham‐nanoFUS. Behavioral testing was then repeated after treatment.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Active‐nanoFUS neuromodulation reduced aggressive behavior and agitation in male mice, as compared to sham‐treated controls. Treatment with active‐nanoFUS increased the time male mice spent in social‐non‐aggressive behaviors.

sec.title: Interpretation
sec.p: Our results show that neuromodulation with active‐nanoFUS may be a potential therapeutic tool for the treatment of neuropsychiatric symptoms, with special focus on agitation and aggressive behaviors. Further studies are necessary to establish cellular, molecular and long‐term behavioral changes following treatment with nanoFUS.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a chronic and progressive neurodegenerative disorder, characterized by impairments in memory and cognition, the accumulation of extracellular amyloid‐β plaques, intraneuronal fibrillar depositions of tau protein, and neuronal loss. 1 AD is the most common form of dementia, with a global prevalence expected to reach over 100 million cases by 2050. 2 Along with cognitive changes, patients with AD often experience neuropsychiatric symptoms, such as depression, delusions, and agitation. 3 , 4

Agitation is a multifactorial behavioral syndrome that includes excessive motor activity (e.g., pacing and restlessness), verbal (e.g., yelling and shouting), and/or physical aggression (e.g., grabbing, hitting others and/or self, destroying property). 5 Agitation increases with disease severity, from approximately 10% in mild cognitive impairment, 6 up to 50% in patients with moderate‐to‐severe AD, 7 affecting 48–88% of institutionalized patients. 3 , 8 Patients with AD and associated agitation are challenging to treat, pose a high caregiver burden, have a poor quality of life and an increased rate of institutionalization. 4 , 9 Also, standard medical treatments with antipsychotic medications may be costly, lead to undesirable side effects, and increase mortality risk. 3 , 10 Thus, the development of novel therapeutics tailored to address these symptoms is paramount.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies in patients with AD and agitation have shown widespread cortical atrophy and loss of white matter integrity in limbic and frontal cortical regions. 11 , 12 , 13 This correlates with reduced metabolic activity in frontal, temporal, and cingulate cortices, 14 , 15 , 16 as well as an increased activation of the amygdala. 17 These results are in line with previous studies suggesting that agitation and aggressive behavior occur as a result of a reduced top‐down inhibitory control of frontal areas over the amygdala, which becomes hyperactive. 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 In fact, the modulation or inactivation of the amygdala have been reported to successfully reduce agitation and aggressive behaviors in distinct patient populations. 22 , 23 , 24

Targeted neuromodulation with ultrasound‐sensitive nanodroplets coupled with Focused Ultrasound (nanoFUS) is a safe, reproducible and attractive minimally invasive tool that does not compromise the integrity of the blood–brain barrier (BBB). In addition, anesthetic‐loaded nanodroplets are highly stable and have a prolonged half‐life compared to microbubbles. 25 , 26 , 27 The release and distribution of pharmaceuticals loaded onto nanodroplets only occur above the vaporization threshold and are pressure‐dependent, achieving precise spatial resolution. 25 Furthermore, it is possible to predict the extent of the distribution via the acoustic emissions detected during sonications 25 and investigate the successful treatment via the behavioral modifications observed in rodents. 26 , 27

Mouse models of AD are useful for the development of novel therapeutics, as they can present with amyloid and/or tau pathology and behavioral changes that mimic AD symptoms. Agitation, as detected by increased motor activity in homecage or in the open‐field test (OFT), has been reported to occur spontaneously in several AD mouse models. 28 Male mice with AD pathology frequently show aggressive behaviors towards same‐sex conspecifics, 29 a feature not observed in females (for a review see Kosel et al. 28 ). The TgCRND8 mouse model of AD 30 encodes a double mutant form of the human amyloid precursor protein 695, 30 presenting amyloid pathology and cognitive deficits by 3 months of age, and are extensively used for the study of novel therapeutics. 31 , 32 , 33 , 34 , 35 In this study, we apply nanoFUS for the first time in a mouse model of AD to test the hypothesis that bilateral intra‐amygdala nanoFUS neuromodulation will reduce agitation and aggressive behavior in TgCRND8 mice.

sec.title: Animals included and husbandry
sec.p: All procedures were approved by the Sunnybrook Research Institute Animal Care Committee and were in agreement with the guidelines of the Canadian Council on Animal Care and the Animals for Research Act of Ontario. Male and female 3 months old (at onset of experiments) transgenic CRND8 (TgCRND8) mice from the Centre for Research in Neurodegenerative Disease were used (12 female, 14 male). Mice were bred and housed at the Sunnybrook Research Institute (Toronto, Canada). TgCRND8 mice were maintained on a C57BL/6 and C3H hybrid background, encoding a double mutant form of the human amyloid precursor protein 695 (i.e., Swedish [KM670/671NL] and Indiana [V717F]) under the control of the hamster prion (PrP gene) promoter. 30 TgCRND8 mice amyloid pathology has been well characterized in various immunization paradigms. 31 , 32 , 36 At the onset of the experiments, TgCRND8 mice were transferred to an inverted 12 h light cycle housing room with optimal conditions of temperature and humidity and kept single‐housed in regular mouse cages containing nest material and environmental enrichments, with free access to food and water. Single housing was necessary for the development of isolation‐induced aggressive behavior. 37 , 38 BALB/cAnNCrl (Charles River Laboratories Canada) of the same sex and age at the time of behavioral testing were used as intruders. These mice were group housed (minimum of 2, maximum of 5 animals/cage) in regular mouse cages containing nest material and environmental enrichments with free access to food and water, and maintained in optimal conditions of temperature and humidity in an inverted 12 h light cycle.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: Twenty‐six 3‐month‐old male and female TgCRND8 mice were single housed for 3 weeks in an inverted 12 h light cycle housing room, for the development of the isolation‐induced aggressive behavior. Following the isolation period, mice were tested in the Resident‐Intruder Test (RIT) in 4 distinct encounters with intruders, followed by the open‐field test (OFT) for the assessment of locomotor activity and motor agitation. Aggressive behavior was present in all male mice, but not in females after 3 weeks of single housing. Animals were then treated with active‐ or sham‐nanoFUS (Females [active n = 8, sham n = 4], Males [active n = 10, sham = 4]) targeting the amygdala bilaterally. Mice in the active‐nanoFUS group received pentobarbital‐loaded nanodroplets, while animals in the sham‐nanoFUS group were treated with empty nanodroplets. They were then evaluated using the 18‐points neurological test 39 (details in the Behavioral Testing below), and tested on 2 additional RIT, followed by an additional OFT. Vaginal cytology was performed in all females to determine the stage of the estrous cycle. Figure 1A illustrates the study design.

caption.p: Study design. (A) Treating agitation/aggressive behavior in TgCRND8 mice with ultrasound‐sensitive nanodroplets (nanoFUS) targeting the amygdala. After 3 weeks of single housing, animals were tested 4 times in the resident‐intruder test (RIT) and one time in the open‐field test (OFT) for the assessment of baseline levels of aggressive behavior and motor agitation. TgCRND8 mice were then treated with active‐ or sham‐nanoFUS, followed by an evaluation using the 18‐points composite neurological test (NT), and retested in the RIT and OFT for after treatment measures of behavior. (B) Illustration of the LP100 focused ultrasound system used in this study. (C) Illustrations of coronal and sagittal sections of the mouse brain showing the eight focal spots used to cover the amygdala bilaterally (4 focal spots per hemisphere).

sec.title: Behavioral testing
sec.p: Behavioral testing was conducted under red light (active time of the animals' day/night cycle), as mice were kept in an inverted light cycle. Sessions were video‐recorded and analyzed by an expert observer blinded to treatment allocation using the EthoWatcher® software. 40

sec.title: Resident‐intruder test
sec.p: The RIT, a standard test for aggression in mice, was used to investigate aggressive behavior. 37 Mice were single housed for 3 weeks for the development of isolation‐induced aggression (i.e., Resident). Thereafter, during each trial, resident mice were exposed to an intruder (i.e., unfamiliar adult mouse of the same‐sex) in its home cage for 5 min. Behaviors were categorized in social or non‐social, and further subdivided in social‐aggressive (i.e., bites/attacks, threats, mounting, and pursuit), social‐non‐aggressive (i.e., whole body social sniffing and whole body social grooming), non‐social‐towards‐self (i.e., self‐grooming), and non‐social‐towards‐environment (i.e., exploring, eating, digging, and resting).

sec.title: Open‐field test
sec.p: The OFT was used to access motor agitation, as previously described. 41 Mice were placed in the open‐field apparatus (50 cm × 50 cm × 38 cm) and allowed to freely explore it for 5 min. Between sessions, the OF was cleaned with virox and ethanol solutions and dried with a paper towel. The total distance (cm) traveled during the test and average speed (cm/sec) were scored. To better investigate motor agitation, speed fluctuations during the test were individually calculated using the standard deviation of each animal's velocity.

sec.title: 18‐Points composite neurological test
sec.p: Mice were assessed in the 18‐points neurological test to determine whether they were fully recovered from anesthesia prior to further testing. Scoring was conducted according to a standard classification system 39 evaluating neurological responses in 6 domains: (i) Spontaneous activity (i.e., ability to freely and spontaneously move, and approach all four walls of the cage during 5 min of observation); (ii) Symmetry in the movement of the four limbs (i.e., the animal is briefly held in the air by the tail to observe whether all four limbs extend symmetrically); (iii) Forepaw Outstretching (i.e., the animal is briefly placed on the edge of the cage lid, while being held by the tail to observe whether both forelimbs outstretch, and the animal walks symmetrically on forepaws); (iv) Climbing (i.e., the animal is placed on the wall of a wired cage to observe climbing and the strength of attachment to the wire); (v) Body proprioception (i.e., the animal is gently touched with a blunt stick on each side of the hind body to observe the reaction of turning the head towards the stimulus); (vi) Response to vibrissae touch (i.e., the animal's vibrissae is gently touched with a blunt stick on each side of the face, starting from the back of the head, to observe the reaction of turning the head towards the stimulus). Lower scores indicate neurological impairment. Only animals presenting normal neurological activity were included in this study, as neurological impairment would alter the animal's response on the behavioral testing and the recorded results could be potentially misinterpreted.

sec.title: Magnetic resonance guided focused ultrasound with ultrasound‐sensitive nanodroplets
sec.p: Mice were anesthetized with Isoflurane and a 22 gauge tail vein catheter was placed. Depilatory cream was used to remove hair from the scalp, and ultrasound gel was applied to enable sufficient coupling with the system. The animal was then positioned supine on top of an MRI‐compatible ultrasound positioning system. Using a 7‐Tesla small bore MRI scanner (BioSpec 70/30 USR, Bruker, Billerica, MA, USA), T2‐weighted images were acquired for precise targeting (TR = 800 ms, TE = 3 ms, matrix = 256 × 256, Slice Thickness = 1.5 mm). The ultrasound‐sensitive nanodroplets were fabricated as previously described. 26 , 27 Briefly, definity‐based (Lantheus Medical Imaging, USA) nanodroplets with lipid shell and liquid decafluorobutane (Synquest Labs, USA) core were synthesized using a modified condensation technique 26 , 27 and loaded with pentobarbital (25 μg/mL, Sigma Aldrich Millipore Sigma, USA). The final nanodroplet solution was passed slowly through a cold 0.8 μm sterile syringe filter (Minisart Syringe Filter, Sartorius, Germany) to remove erroneous large droplets. Nanodroplets were delivered via the tail vein catheter in a slow bolus (0.1 mL per injection, 1 injection per hemisphere), followed by a 100 μL saline flush, 10 sec after the start of FUS sonication. 26 , 27

Focused ultrasound was delivered using an ultrasound system (a prototype of LP100, FUS Instruments Inc., Toronto, ON, Canada; Fig. 1B) with a spherically focused transducer (1.78 MHz center frequency, 60 mm radius of curvature, 75 mm external diameter with circular cut‐out of 20 mm diameter in the center of the transducer), with a coaxially aligned polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) hydrophone embedded in the center, used to detect acoustic activity from vaporizing nanodroplets. The focal pressure was calibrated in water using a planar fiber optic hydrophone with an active tip diameter of 10 μm (Precision Acoustics Ltd., Dorset, UK). The system includes a tank of degassed and deionized water through which the transducer is moved using a motorized positioning system. The surface of the water is coupled to a polyimide membrane which in turn is coupled, using ultrasound gel, to the animal's skull. The spatial coordinates of the LP100 system were co‐registered with the 7 T MRI scanner, allowing the target to be determined using axial T2w images. In the current study, eight focal spots were chosen to cover the amygdala bilaterally (4 focal spots per hemisphere, Fig. 1C), where each ultrasound focus had a volume of 0.8 × 0.8 × 3 mm. The sonication parameters were selected based on previous work 25 , 26 , 27 , 42 , 43 showing optimal nanodroplet vaporization without disrupting the BBB, and were applied using 10 msec bursts, at a repetition frequency of 1 Hz, for 180 sec, starting 10 sec before nanodroplet injection. For all sonications, the acoustic pressure amplitude was increased in a stepwise manner, starting at 1.0 MPa, with 0.012 MPa increments until subharmonic emissions were detected, signaling nanodroplet vaporization. At the end of the procedures, animals returned to their homecages and were allowed to recover for 1 h.

sec.title: Vaginal cytology
sec.p: Vaginal lavage was performed in all female mice on the final day of experiments, by applying 100 μL of sterile saline solution via a 200 μL pipette. After collection, the samples were stained with Giemsa and evaluated under light microscopy. 44 In the last day of the experiments, 14% of females were in estrus, 43% in diestrus, 29% in metestrus, and 14% in proestrus. There were no statistical differences in the estrous cycle, and the stages of the estrous cycle were included in all statistical models as fixed effects.

sec.title: Statistical analyses
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed using the packages survival (version 3.2–13) and lme4 (version 1.1–23) in R (version 3.6.1; https://www.r‐project.org/). Latency to Attack and percentage of animals attacking were analyzed using Cox Proportional Hazards Model and Pearson's chi‐squared test with Yates' continuity correction. For the remaining behaviors, linear mixed effect models were chosen, as they allow for the analysis of the relationship between a response variable (i.e., dependent variable) and one or more variables and their interactions (i.e., independent variables, or fixed effect). In these models, behavior of interest was set as the dependent variable, timepoint (i.e., trials 1–6) as fixed effect, and subject as a random effect. For females, the stage of the estrous cycle was added to the model as a fixed effect. The nanoFUS target pressure was evaluated using t‐test. Where applicable, data are presented as mean ± standard error. The level of significance was set at p < 0.05.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Male and female TgCRND8 mice were randomly assigned to receive active‐ or sham‐nanoFUS neuromodulation targeting the amygdala bilaterally (Fig. 2A). The target pressure was determined by ramping the ultrasound pressure until the onset of subharmonic activity was detected by the hydrophone. Ultrasound transmission through the skull is known to correlate with the rodent's weight. 45 Males were heavier than females and required greater target pressure (females: 20.6 ± 3 g, 2 ± 0.2 MPa; males: 27.8 ± 1.9 g, 2.1 ± 0.2 MPa; t = −2.11, df = 24, p = 0.045; Fig. 2B,C). Following treatment, animals were allowed to recover for 1 h in their homecage, followed by an evaluation with the 18‐point neurological scale. One male mouse presented neurological deficits and was excluded from further analyses (i.e., reduced spontaneous motor activity with the animal barely moving in the home cage; slow response to body and vibrissae stimuli). Animals were then tested in the RIT and OFT.

caption.p: NanoFUS treatment and resident‐intruder test. Treatment of aggressive behavior/agitation in the TgCRND8 mouse model of Alzheimer's Disease using Magnetic Resonance Guided Focused Ultrasound with Ultrasound‐Sensitive Nanodroplets (nanoFUS). (A). Axial T2 weighted magnetic resonance images showing an amygdala bilaterally targeted with nanoFUS. (B). The target pressure required to reach subharmonic activity corresponded to the animals' weight. (C) Males were heavier and required a greater target pressure to reach subharmonic activity compared to females. (D) There were no differences between animals at baseline measures on the latency to attack and the proportion of animals attacking. (E) Active‐nanoFUS (Active) treatment resulted in an increased latency to attack and a reduced proportion of animals attacking as compared to sham‐nanoFUS group (Sham). (F) There were no differences between animals before treatment on the number of attacks performed in each trial. (G) Active‐nanoFUS neuromodulation resulted in a reduced number of attacks as compared to sham‐nanoFUS control. Significance codes: *p < 0.05; **p < 0.01; ns: non‐significant.

sec.title: Resident‐intruder test
sec.p: Before treatment, no differences were found between male mice allocated to the active‐ or sham‐nanoFUS groups in the latency to attack (β = −0.4, exp = 0.6, SE = 0.3, z = −1.4, p = 0.174) or the proportion of attacking animals (χ 2 = 1.6, df = 1, p = 0.205; Fig. 2D). After treatment, male mice in the active‐nanoFUS group had a significantly higher latency to attack compared to sham‐treated controls (β = −1.6, exp = 0.2, SE = 0.6, z = −2.4, p = 0.017). In addition, the proportion of animals that attacked the intruders was smaller in the active‐nanoFUS group compared to sham‐treated animals (χ 2 = 4.5, df = 1, p = 0.034, Fig. 2E).

No differences between groups were observed before treatment in the number of attacks per trial (β = 2.4, SE = 3.6, df = 11, p = 0.506). Both groups showed the same progressive increase in the number of attacks, such that both groups attacked more times on trial 4 than in previous trials (β = −10, SE = 4.5, df = 55, p = 0.029; Fig. 2F). After nanoFUS neuromodulation, a significant reduction in the number of attacks was observed, with male animals in the active‐nanoFUS group attacking less compared to animals in the sham‐nanoFUS group (β = −15, SE = 5.4, df = 55, p = 0.007; Fig. 2G). No female mice showed aggressive behaviors in the RIT (Table 1).

caption.p: Behavioral response in the resident‐intruder test (RIT) and open‐field test (OFT).

fn.p: Values in the table represent mean ± standard deviation.

sec.p: Before treatment, no differences were observed between groups on the percentage of time spent in non‐social behaviors (male: β = 4.4, SE = 4.4, df = 11, p = 0.332; female: β = 1, SE = 3.8, df = 59, p = 0.795) or social non‐aggressive behaviors (male: β = −6.3, SE = 4.3, df = 11, p = 0.170; female: β = 19, SE = 3.9, df = 59, p = 0.795). After nanoFUS neuromodulation, male mice in the active‐nanoFUS group presented a significant increase in the percentage of time spent in non‐social behaviors (β = −14, SE = 5.4, df = 55, p = 0.011) and social non‐aggressive behaviors (β = −13.6, SE = 6.6, df = 55, p = 0.044), in relation to the sham‐nanoFUS group. No differences were observed between treatment groups in females (non‐social behaviors: β = −1.6, SE = 8.8, df = 59, p = 0.857; social non‐aggressive behaviors: β = −1.69, SE = 8.89, df = 59, p = 0.706, Table 1).

sec.title: Open‐field test
sec.p: No differences between groups were observed at baseline in the total distance traveled (male: β = −1591.5, SE = 906.4, df = 11, p = 0.106, female: β = −77.7, SE = 1052.6, df = 9, p = 0.942, Figs. 3A,B) or in speed fluctuation (male: β = −5.2, SE = 3.2, df = 10, p = 0.135, female: β = −0.7, SE = 3.5, df = 8, p = 0.838, Fig. 3C, Table 1). After nanoFUS neuromodulation, male mice in the active‐nanoFUS group traveled significantly less than sham‐treated controls (β = −1520.9, SE = 648.2, df = 11, p = 0.038; Fig. 3A) and presented a significant reduction in speed fluctuation (β = 0.3, SE = 0.1, df = 18, p = 0.031, Fig. 3C). No differences were observed between treatment groups composed of female mice (total distance: β = 1455.0, SE = 858.8, df = 10, p = 0.121, speed fluctuation: β = 4.4, SE = 3.3, df = 9, p = 0.224, Fig. 3, Table 1).

caption.p: Open‐field test. Treatment of aggressive behavior/agitation in the TgCRND8 mouse model of Alzheimer's Disease using Magnetic Resonance Guided Focused Ultrasound and pentobarbital‐loaded Ultrasound‐Sensitive Nanodroplets (nanoFUS). (A) No difference between groups was observed before treatment in the Total Distance Traveled. Treatment with active‐nanoFUS reduced the total distance traveled in males. (B) Illustration of the automated tracking for each sex (i.e., male or female), group (i.e., active‐ or sham‐nanoFUS), and timepoint (i.e. baseline or after treatment). (C) No difference between groups was observed at baseline in speed fluctuation. Treatment with active‐nanoFUS reduced speed fluctuation in males. Significance code: *p < 0.05; ns: non‐significant.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Agitation and aggressive behaviors are distressing neuropsychiatric symptoms frequently observed in patients with AD. 5 , 6 , 7 These symptoms pose a great risk for self‐injury and injury to caregivers, result in high rates of institutionalization, and lead to great suffering for patients and families. 9 , 46 Current pharmacological therapies have limited efficacy and a high potential for severe side effects. 10 Thus, there is a growing need to develop novel therapeutics that are tailored to safely and effectively reduce agitation in AD. Transgenic animal models of AD, such as the TgCRND8 mice used in our study, are useful for the development of novel therapies, as behavioral responses following treatment can be thoroughly investigated.

Recently, our group has demonstrated the potential of using focused ultrasound as a non‐invasive neuromodulatory method to vaporize drug‐loaded ultrasound‐sensitive nanodroplets, release their content in specific brain targets, and alter local neural activity. 26 , 27 In this study, we sought to investigate the effects of nanoFUS neuromodulation to reduce neuropsychiatric symptoms, specifically agitation and aggressive behavior, in the TgCRND8 mouse model of AD. In contrast to systemic drug administration, the delivery via nanoFUS offers the possibility of targeting only a discrete brain target, while preserving the surrounding areas. 25

Nanodroplets firstly respond to ultrasound by being converted from liquid droplet into gaseous microbubbles (i.e., vaporization), and then by expanding, becoming unstable, and collapsing inwards from the inertia of the surrounding fluid (i.e., inertial cavitation). 47 Stable cavitation is fundamental for enhancing drug delivery and distribution, and can be controlled via real‐time acoustic monitoring. 47 Small lipophilic drugs, such as the pentobarbital, do not require the BBB to be breached to penetrate the brain tissue. However, the encapsulation in nanodroplets is fundamental for a localized and precise delivery. Although previous studies have shown possible BBB disruption during nanodroplets sonication, 48 , 49 our recent work using contrast‐enhanced MRI has shown that the blood–brain barrier remains intact after exposure to nanoFUS using the sonication parameters applied in this study. 26

It is important to highlight that this is the first study investigating nanoFUS as a direct way of modulating behavior in a mouse model of AD. Thus, our current results may be considered a starting point for the development of new treatments for neuropsychiatric symptoms in AD models. The RIT is considered to be the standard test for investigating aggressive behaviors in rodents. 50 As a result, it has been extensively used in studies involving both wild‐type animals and transgenic mice with AD pathology. 28 , 50 , 51 In this test, a resident mouse is confronted by a same‐sex intruder in its homecage and both the latency to the first attack and number of attacks are recorded. In general, the aggressive behavior increases with repeated exposure to the RIT. 52 , 53 Before treatment, we observed that male mice expressed this well‐established behavioral pattern in the RIT, characterized by a progressive increase in aggressive behavior over time, a lower latency to attack, and several attacks in each encounter. Following nanoFUS neuromodulation, there was a significant reduction in aggressive behavior in the active‐nanoFUS group, as compared to sham‐nanoFUS controls (Fig. 2).

A critical aspect to consider is that the sham‐treated group underwent anesthesia and were treated with FUS with empty nanodroplets. This group was selected instead of animals exposed only to anesthesia to control for the possible effect of nanodroplet vaporization and the passage of the FUS beams through the brain. In females, aggressive behavior is typically observed in the context of maternal aggression 54 , 55 and not in the RIT. Previous studies in transgenic female mice with AD pathology tested in the RIT have shown an absence of aggressive behavior, a phenotype that was also observed in our study. 28 , 51 , 56 , 57 , 58

The time spent on social‐non‐aggressive behaviors is another important feature evaluated in our study, as social impairment is frequently observed in AD patients. 59 The pattern of social behaviors has been found to be correlated with the concentration of amyloid peptides in the frontal cortex in mouse models of AD. 56 Our animals were approximately 4 months old during behavioral testing, an age during which amyloid accumulation is clearly present in the frontal cortex. 30 As a result, it is possible to reason that the pattern of social behaviors presented here may be a product of amyloid pathology. Interestingly, treatment with active‐nanoFUS increases the time male mice spend on social‐non‐aggressive behavior, suggesting that this neuromodulation technique has the potential to simultaneously treat several distinct domains of neuropsychiatric symptoms.

The assessment of hyperactivity using standard tests, such as the OFT, has been shown to be reliable for studying agitation in mice. 28 , 60 , 61 While several transgenic mouse models of AD have been described as presenting hyperactivity, 60 motor activity was found to be normal 62 or even reduced in previous work, depending on the strain tested 56 (for review see Lalonde et al. 61 ). It has been postulated that distinct genetic backgrounds, husbandry practices, baseline levels of anxiety‐like behavior, along with methodologic factors related to the apparatus, could result in the different levels of agitation observed in those studies. 28 , 61 We observed a significant reduction in motor agitation in male mice receiving active‐nanoFUS neuromodulation, in comparison with the sham‐treated controls, as measured by reductions in the total distance traveled and speed fluctuations.

It has been shown that the delivery of pentobarbital (an agonist of GABA receptor type A 63 , 64 ) via nanoFUS is capable of reducing immediate early gene expression in the target area. 27 The systemic delivery of this drug decreases serotonin turnover, thus increasing the extracellular concentration of this neurotransmitter throughout the brain. 65 These results are in line with the body of literature showing reductions in motor agitation and aggressive behaviors following functional neurosurgery and neuromodulation treatments that reduce amygdala activity 22 , 23 , 24 (for a review see Gouveia et al. 19 ). Also, it is believed that agitation and aggressive behavior occur when there is an imbalance in serotonin transmission leading to a reduced top‐down inhibitory control of the limbic system, 66 , 67 subsequently increasing amygdala activity and dopamine release. 18 , 19 , 23 Thus, it is possible that nanoFUS neuromodulation reduces agitation and aggressive behavior via two simultaneous mechanisms: Reducing amygdala activity and increasing a top‐down inhibitory control of the limbic system. Interestingly, the acute administration of dopamine (i.e., D2) and serotonin (i.e., 5HT‐1 and 5HT‐2) receptor antagonists reduce aggressive behavior in male Tg‐AD mice undergoing the RIT, as reflected by an increase in the latency to attack and a reduction in the number of attacks per trial. 57 Further studies investigating the involvement of the monoamines in the mechanism of action of nanoFUS are still required.

Altogether, our results show that neuromodulation with active‐nanoFUS may be a potential therapeutic tool for the treatment of neuropsychiatric symptoms, with special focus on agitation and aggressive behaviors. Further studies are necessary to establish cellular, molecular, and long‐term behavioral changes following treatment with nanoFUS.
